SA Tourism in ICU

By: Joy Summers | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Summary We are now in lockdown level one – The president speaks about our new growth path. Tourism is one of the pillars of the recovery plan but right now this is an industry that despite governme

Unique Selling Point:
Great case studies and great visuals

Summary:
Inbound Tourism generates R82bn for South Africa’s economy, it is one of our largest export earners, but it’s on its knees with 66% of the market unable to enter South Africa- the industry becomes unviable for many operators and after 6 months of no business tourism 40 % of the businesses are in danger of folding. International tour operators are dropping SA from their brochures and marketing and international research says SA will only recover in 2024.


Further information:
The tourism minister is concerned after her recent visit to Limpopo where she can see for herself what is happening. We will try and get an interview with her or the tourism business council CEO Tshifiwe Tshivenga

Tinyiko Hlungwani, is the manager of Nahakwe Lodge, a 4-star venue located 90 km north of Polokwane. Owned by the local community of the Mamaila Kolobetona Traditional Authority it’s a showcase of a modern community-owned tourism enterprise. Tinyiko’s journey into tourism started as a petrol attendant, followed by a housekeeping position to hospitality management over nearly 18 years at Shiluvari Lakeside Lodge, on the Levubu in the foothills of the Luonde Mountains. For her, the survival of the industry is non-negotiable. “Lockdown affected us a lot in terms of salaries. A lot of families have been affected, 24 people (counting myself) have lost their income, and most of us are supporting families”

Madeleine Hedem, Tamrich Tours started as a guide at Gold Reef City and then became a tour operator dealing with Southern African countries. She opened Tamrich Tours in 1999. Her key market is the Middle East known for predominantly luxury travel. Cancellations started upon the announcement of South Africa’s lockdown, and soon she lost her Forward Book. She has a small team who have started working on a rotational basis, having initially relied on TERS! Her concern as the opening of borders has been a total miscommunication in that “realistically South Africa may only operate as a tourism destination in the second half of 2021”.

Martin Wiest, Chief Executive, Tourvest Destination Management Company, South Africa’s largest Destination Management Company. Responsible for handling on an annual basis +/- 200 000 tourists coming to South Africa. In March 2020, the company had half a billion Rand on their Forward Book; today they have R60 million left and it is fast evaporating. The used to receive 1000 – 1500 bookings per day; now it is between 5-10 if they are lucky! They have downscaled their staff (which runs across 5 x different companies) by 50%; morale has dropped & those remaining are traumatised. International visitors are critical for the livelihood of smaller, remote areas where jobs have been created because of tourism.
Martin says “It is critical that we get the opening right; in view of the future & forward bookings. The borders need to open in a logical, predictable fashion so we create TRUST with our source markets. South Africa has always been an aspirational holiday destination. We now need to fight for market share against other destinations like Australia & NZ for example”.

Tourism in ICU Final script TX Sunday 6th December 2020 FACT CHECKED

Commentary One
Closed indefinitely: The Michelangelo Sandton. The Hyatt Rosebank, closed till October 2021. The iconic Mount Nelson, partially opening December. Zimbali Lodge- in business rescue.

LINK
As Covid19 spread across the world, the tourism industry watched in trepidation, but back in March, few could imagine the devastation that lay ahead

Commentary two
Marcel Von Aulock is the CEO of Tsogo Sun Hotels – the leading hotel group in Africa

Marcel Von Aulock
It’s fair to say no one in the world has ever seen anything like this. When the hard lockdown came we had to close 103 hotels in 3 days, and a lot of these buildings had never been closed in their life. We have hotels that haven’t closed their doors in 40 years, and you don’t have a plan for how you close that many properties that quickly, everything from food in the fridges, the water systems and so on
Claire
How did the week feel like, having to shut down?
Marcel
I mean it was surreal, it wasn’t a time of moping, it was a time of scrambling, you are dealing with banks, and what are you going to do with employees and suppliers, and you realize your revenue is collapsing fast, but you can’t actually understand that it is going to zero. There is no way that a multibillion rand, biggest hotel group in Africa should go to zero revenue in the space of a week like that

Commentary Three
A few hours before our interview, Von Aulock had presented the group results. Revenue was down a massive R1.8 billion rand

Marcel
So there’s R1.8 billion of revenue that just disappeared, so in 6 months we lost more money than we made in the entire previous year

LINK
The numbers are frightening, thousands of retrenchments, hundreds of hotel rooms empty, and revenue decimated

Commentary Four
These are the Sandton offices of Tourvest, the biggest tour operator in the Southern Hemisphere. The rows of empty desks, the calendars still stuck on March, the computers stored away, are the only traces of around 2500 jobs lost in just this one company.

Martin Wiest is the CEO.

Martin
Remember this is now a start-up industry, it’s no longer an industry that you rebuild. You have a start-up industry with thirty-year’s experience

Commentary five
He says tourism is an apex industry- and its destruction, ripples outwards

Martin
Now what does it mean to be an APEX industry? If you take for example car manufacturing in SA. The car rental industry buys 50 000 cars and this year they buy less than 10 000 cars, the same applies to wine making. In a normal year we have 1.8 million tourists, they come for on average ten days and drink a bottle of wine a day, so that is 18 million bottles of wine they don’t drink them at the moment

Commentary Six
And as this apex industry caved in, it’s taken the livelihoods of around a million people with it

Claire
How has this impacted your entire team?
Marcel
There is the corporate CEO answer that says we have managed the cost, we have reduced the cash burn, we have relooked at our structures, and there is the not corporate answer that says how do you take a business and you make all these people just go home?

And they have given you everything, and then as you start opening up who gets to come back? How do you arrange the shift? You can give no certainty as to when this thing is going to turn and you start with a we are all in this together for three months and becomes four months, becomes five and then you are sitting on nine months…

Up sound
Cars on rutted road- children filling in potholes

Commentary seven
This is the road to Nahakwe lodge in Limpopo, close to Giyani. Local children fill the potholes for change. There is an argument about which government department should fix it, so it stays like this, a deterrent to potential visitors.

Nahakwe reopened its doors in August, but the four star rooms are barely occupied. Moses Mokoro is assistant manager

Moses Mokoro
By next year December if we are still open, it will really be a miracle



Commentary eight
Lodge manager Tinyiko Hlungwane’s story is a prime example of just how tourism can uplift rural people. After school, there was no money for further studies, so she found a job at a garage

Tinyiko
I was a petrol attendant I was checking oil, pumping tyres, washing windscreens

Commentary nine
But an opportunity at a lodge launched her career, and after learning the ropes she was promoted to manage it. In 2016 she came to Nahakwe, built by the department of tourism on community land. Until lockdown they were doing well.

Tinyiko
Sometimes I keep myself motivated but sometimes I lose it. I wake up not knowing what to do. It’s very depressing, especially mid- week, sitting with no income. I look at my staff, they don’t have enough money for transport …what about the food at home. We are really in trouble

Commentary Ten
She used to take her international clients to the Ribola art route in a nearby village. The Ribola route supports potters, textile workers and woodcarvers, but they too are struggling.

Kenny Nonyama is one of the woodcarvers

Kenny
This sculpture is talking about the pandemic of this Corona Virus. So the lady here is representing the world of South Africa. This is a big rock, showing the challenge the world is facing. This man is representing our president, trying to pull this challenge away from people.

Commentary eleven
The rock was lifted off the industry when President Ramaphosa opened the borders in mid-November with strict safety protocols. South Africa’s magnificence was once again on display

Music montage

But it may be too late for any quick turnarounds

Martin Weist
Many of my friends said when we opened up our borders, yay your business is back to normal, but the truth is we still don’t have any tourists in country. Today we have six people in country under normal circumstances we have 4- 5000 people in country simultaneously


Commentary twelve
Former special advisor to Derek Hanekom, and industry expert Gillian Saunders, says mistakes were made.

Gillian
And when it came to opening our borders, home affairs would say this, Dirco would say that, transport would say this and each of them would have half a story and there was no full story clearly laid out as to what was going to happen
Claire
And what impact did that have?
Gillian
That had the market of foreigners saying sorry we can’t come to South Africa. Cancellations. Uncertainty compounded and compounded.

Commentary thirteen
But, says Saunders, it’s still possible, even with this delay, to get the 21 million tourists the president is aiming for by 2030.

Gillian
I looked at the game lodge industry and protected areas industry, and globally there’s been a number of surveys and we have been the number one choice destination for surveys in Europe and the USA where do you want to go when Covid19 is over…South AFRICA.

Commentary fourteen
That can’t come soon enough for Robert More, founder of a collection of exclusive lodges that depend on high net worth foreigners

Robert
The big issue for me is the lack of dialogue between government and private sector. It’s easy to close something down, its much more difficult to build it up The safari industry was prevented from accepting travelers, and yet it’s an outdoor experience, the covid protocols are easily applied, but the game lodge industry was forgotten about

Commentary fifteen
To survive they have pivoted from an 80% reliance on international business, to 80% local. But to maintain quality, keep staff and reduce their prices, they have had to resort to debt funding.

Robert
This whole last eight months has felt like eight years in terms of how we have had to re-engineer our business.

Commentary sixteen
And their community trust supported by the company, was forced to abandon teaching children, to handing them food parcels.


Robert
So the word we started to use is we have to learn how to hustle

Commentary seventeen
Right now, the whole industry is hustling, hoping to attract the dollars and the Euro’s back to our shores.

Robert
Next year our objective is to break even as an organization, the following year is a recovery from that…. recovery to 2019- hopefully optimistically 2023 more probable 2024

LINK
For optimists in this industry SA now has a small but unique window of opportunity, and they say we must seize it with both hands

Commentary eighteen
And it’s the Australians we could seize it from. David Frost is CEO of SATSA, and a former special advisor to two previous tourism ministers.

David Frost
Australia has a sparse coastline, a rock in the middle and some mangy animals! We have the big five. We have culture, rich history, cuisine and wine and friendly people

Commentary eighteen A
South Africa only gets about two and a half million to Australia’s 9 million tourists, but right now Australia’s borders are virtually closed.

David Frost
For me it should have been the other way around, we should get 9 and the Australians should get 2.5 million!

Commentary nineteen
Frost’s view is that government must prioritize tourism across ALL ministries, and work better with the private sector.

David Frost
The Ozzies are the long haul benchmark in terms of success …they get together at the point of inception and then they strategize together and execute together. We are still in separate movies

Commentary twenty
Spokesperson for the Minister of Tourism- Hlengiwe Nhlabathi-Mokota disagrees

Hlengiwe
Over the last couple of months there has been interaction, that is why I say I disagree with the fact that there is no co-ordination

Commentary Twenty one
She says the minister has called for all stakeholders to come together, they are bidding for conferences, and they are on a marketing campaign

Hlengiwe
So we believe aggressive marketing of our country is going to put us back where the tourism sector is supposed to be

Commentary twenty- two
But until then, for those in tourism, more sleepless nights may still lie ahead.

Marcel
You think about funny things, I woke up in middle night with a sudden cold sweat and I thought we have these beautiful Koi fish in the pond in front of the Palazzo, and it suddenly occurred to me that the hotel is closed, is anyone feeding the fish?!
Claire
Out of all the thousands of things you should be worrying about?
Marcel
They are gorgeous fish, you don’t want to lose them! (they laugh)

THE END 11 03

PROMO ONE
Lockdown decimated the tourism industry, hotels closed, and around a million livelihoods were lost. Now as we reopen our borders, how will tourism recover?

PROMO TWO
President Ramaphosa set a target for 21 million tourists to come to our shores by 2030. Covid 19 delayed that, but now it’s time to rebuild safely

PROMO THREE
Rebuilding our tourism sector could take as long as four years, in the meantime, locals have an opportunity to pick up great deals and support the recovery of the industry.

Gillian I looked at the game lodge industry and protected areas industry, and globally there’s been a number of surveys and we have been the number one choice destination for surveys in Europe and the USA where do you want to go when Covid19 is over…South AFRICA. Commentary fourteen That can’t come soon enough for Robert More, founder of a collection of exclusive lodges that depend on high net worth foreigners Robert The big issue for me is the lack of dialogue between government and private sector. It’s easy to close something down, its much more difficult to build it up The safari industry was prevented from accepting travelers, and yet it’s an outdoor experience, the covid protocols are easily applied, but the game lodge industry was forgotten about Commentary fifteen To survive they have pivoted from an 80% reliance on international business, to 80% local. But to maintain quality, keep staff and reduce their prices, they have had to resort to debt funding. Robert This whole last eight months has felt like eight years in terms of how we have had to re-engineer our business. Commentary sixteen And their community trust supported by the company, was forced to abandon teaching children, to handing them food parcels. Robert So the word we started to use is we have to learn how to hustle Commentary seventeen Right now, the whole industry is hustling, hoping to attract the dollars and the Euro’s back to our shores. Robert Next year our objective is to break even as an organization, the following year is a recovery from that…. recovery to 2019- hopefully optimistically 2023 more probable 2024 LINK For optimists in this industry SA now has a small but unique window of opportunity, and they say we must seize it with both hands Commentary eighteen And it’s the Australians we could seize it from. David Frost is CEO of SATSA, and a former special advisor to two previous tourism ministers. David Frost Australia has a sparse coastline, a rock in the middle and some mangy animals! We have the big five. We have culture, rich history, cuisine and wine and friendly people Commentary eighteen A South Africa only gets about two and a half million to Australia’s 9 million tourists, but right now Australia’s borders are virtually closed. David Frost For me it should have been the other way around, we should get 9 and the Australians should get 2.5 million! Commentary nineteen Frost’s view is that government must prioritize tourism across ALL ministries, and work better with the private sector. David Frost The Ozzies are the long haul benchmark in terms of success …they get together at the point of inception and then they strategize together and execute together. We are still in separate movies Commentary twenty Spokesperson for the Minister of Tourism- Hlengiwe Nhlabathi-Mokota disagrees Hlengiwe Over the last couple of months there has been interaction, that is why I say I disagree with the fact that there is no co-ordination Commentary Twenty one She says the minister has called for all stakeholders to come together, they are bidding for conferences, and they are on a marketing campaign Hlengiwe So we believe aggressive marketing of our country is going to put us back where the tourism sector is supposed to be Commentary twenty- two But until then, for those in tourism, more sleepless nights may still lie ahead. Marcel You think about funny things, I woke up in middle night with a sudden cold sweat and I thought we have these beautiful Koi fish in the pond in front of the Palazzo, and it suddenly occurred to me that the hotel is closed, is anyone feeding the fish?! Claire Out of all the thousands of things you should be worrying about? Marcel They are gorgeous fish, you don’t want to lose them! (they laugh) THE END 11 03 PROMO ONE Lockdown decimated the tourism industry, hotels closed, and around a million livelihoods were lost. Now as we reopen our borders, how will tourism recover? PROMO TWO President Ramaphosa set a target for 21 million tourists to come to our shores by 2030. Covid 19 delayed that, but now it’s time to rebuild safely PROMO THREE Rebuilding our tourism sector could take as long as four years, in the meantime, locals have an opportunity to pick up great deals and support the recovery of the industry. metadata.Summary: Inbound Tourism generates R82bn for South Africa’s economy, it is one of our largest export earners, but it’s on its knees with 66% of the market unable to enter South Africa- the industry becomes unviable for many operators and after 6 months of no business tourism 40 % of the businesses are in danger of folding. International tour operators are dropping SA from their brochures and marketing and international research says SA will only recover in 2024.
metadata.Further information: The tourism minister is concerned after her recent visit to Limpopo where she can see for herself what is happening. We will try and get an interview with her or the tourism business council CEO Tshifiwe Tshivenga Tinyiko Hlungwani, is the manager of Nahakwe Lodge, a 4-star venue located 90 km north of Polokwane. Owned by the local community of the Mamaila Kolobetona Traditional Authority it’s a showcase of a modern community-owned tourism enterprise. Tinyiko’s journey into tourism started as a petrol attendant, followed by a housekeeping position to hospitality management over nearly 18 years at Shiluvari Lakeside Lodge, on the Levubu in the foothills of the Luonde Mountains. For her, the survival of the industry is non-negotiable. “Lockdown affected us a lot in terms of salaries. A lot of families have been affected, 24 people (counting myself) have lost their income, and most of us are supporting families” Madeleine Hedem, Tamrich Tours started as a guide at Gold Reef City and then became a tour operator dealing with Southern African countries. She opened Tamrich Tours in 1999. Her key market is the Middle East known for predominantly luxury travel. Cancellations started upon the announcement of South Africa’s lockdown, and soon she lost her Forward Book. She has a small team who have started working on a rotational basis, having initially relied on TERS! Her concern as the opening of borders has been a total miscommunication in that “realistically South Africa may only operate as a tourism destination in the second half of 2021”. Martin Wiest, Chief Executive, Tourvest Destination Management Company, South Africa’s largest Destination Management Company. Responsible for handling on an annual basis +/- 200 000 tourists coming to South Africa. In March 2020, the company had half a billion Rand on their Forward Book; today they have R60 million left and it is fast evaporating. The used to receive 1000 – 1500 bookings per day; now it is between 5-10 if they are lucky! They have downscaled their staff (which runs across 5 x different companies) by 50%; morale has dropped & those remaining are traumatised. International visitors are critical for the livelihood of smaller, remote areas where jobs have been created because of tourism. Martin says “It is critical that we get the opening right; in view of the future & forward bookings. The borders need to open in a logical, predictable fashion so we create TRUST with our source markets. South Africa has always been an aspirational holiday destination. We now need to fight for market share against other destinations like Australia & NZ for example”.
